This guide connects representations, audio descriptors, score and video annotation, and analytical uses of iAnalyse. It is neither a treatise on musical acoustics nor a fixed analytical method. Its aim is to show how signal processing and multimodal annotation can support musicological work grounded in listening, observation, comparison and interpretation.

The annotation library allows you to save annotations or groups of annotations for reuse in other Documents or other Projects.
Annotations are graphics, text, images or videos that you can add to Documents.

Cursors are somewhat special annotations: they appear in the form of animated graphics based on keyframes. They are used to create playheads that move on a score to the rhythm of the music or annotations that highlight the sequence of several notes or chords.

Layers allow you to organize the annotations of a Document. They are useful for separating multiple levels of analysis, displaying only certain annotations, or controlling their behavior during playback.

A Representation Document allows you to display visualizations of the audio signal or imported data. The representations are superimposed in the form of layers which can be edited independently.

iAnalyse is a music analysis software program that allows you to create listening guides, annotate audiovisual and MIDI documents, and produce data representations. iAnalyse is presented as a workspace into which you import files (audio, video, images, PDF, MIDI, etc.) and use to create visualizations. You can create multiple documents (slideshows, signal representations, videos, scores) in each iAnalyse project. The documents share the same files. iAnalyse runs on two platforms: macOS and iPadOS. Projects are identical on both platforms and are compatible with both systems. Both versions contain exactly the same features. However, their location differs due to differences in how the interaction works.
You can test the beta version via TestFlight (macOS 13 or later required). The iPadOS version will follow later. Beta Program

This page describes the audio descriptors computed by iAnalyse.

Audio files are converted through the current analysis pipeline, then descriptors are computed frame by frame. Time-domain descriptors use the frame’s signal directly. Spectral descriptors use a dedicated FFT that returns linear magnitudes, separate from the FFT used to display the spectrogram. Differential descriptors compare the current frame with the previous frame. Typical pipeline: Audio -> resampling 44100 Hz -> decoupage en fenetres -> fenetre d'analyse -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> descripteurs spectraux For stereo descriptors: Audio stereo -> extraction des deux premiers canaux -> decoupage synchronise -> calcul L/R ou MID/SIDE iAnalyse data graphs use a simplified display scale. Some descriptors naturally fall within 0...1; others use a maxRange or minRange for display.

Peak Frequency finds the spectral bin with the highest magnitude and returns its center frequency. It therefore represents the dominant frequency in the frame, without sub-bin interpolation or perceptual pitch estimation.
Signal mono -> fenetre d'analyse -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> recherche du maximum -> frequence du bin

Use it to follow a dominant frequency, resonance, prominent fundamental or stable spectral peak. It is less reliable for noisy textures, dense chords or sounds whose fundamental is not the strongest peak.
RMS Amplitude measures the average signal energy in the frame. Unlike peak amplitude, RMS better represents local average power.
Signal mono -> fenetre temporelle -> carre des echantillons -> moyenne -> racine carree
Use it to follow dynamics, crescendos, energy changes and relatively silent regions. It also underlies other measures such as Loudness and Onset Strength.
Spectral Centroid computes the spectrum’s frequency center of gravity. Higher values indicate that energy is concentrated at higher frequencies.
Signal mono -> fenetre d'analyse -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> ponderation par frequence -> moyenne ponderee
It is useful for tracking brightness, filtering, timbral changes and the overall evolution of the spectrum. In electroacoustic music, it can clearly reveal transitions between dark and bright sounds.
Spectral Crest measures the ratio of the spectral maximum to the spectral mean. The calculation excludes the DC bin so that DC or very low-frequency energy does not bias the result.
Signal mono -> fenetre d'analyse -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> suppression DC -> maximum / moyenne
It distinguishes a spectrum with a dominant peak from one with more evenly distributed energy. Use it to distinguish pitched sounds and resonances from more diffuse spectral masses.
Spectral Decrease measures the overall decline in spectral magnitudes relative to the first bin. A pronounced value indicates a steep decrease in energy with frequency.
Signal mono -> fenetre d'analyse -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> comparaison au premier bin -> normalisation par energie hors DC
It can help identify dark, damped spectra or spectra concentrated in the bass. It is also useful for observing the evolution of low-pass filtering or spectral decay.
Spectral Flatness compares the geometric and arithmetic means of the spectrum. A value near 1 indicates a flat, noise-like spectrum; a value near 0 indicates a more tonal or peaked spectrum.
Signal mono -> fenetre d'analyse -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> moyenne geometrique / moyenne arithmetique
Use it to distinguish noisy, breathy or granular sounds from harmonic or resonant sounds. It can also support segmentation by texture type.
Spectral Flux measures the distance between two consecutive spectra. It accounts for both increases and decreases in spectral energy.
Fenetre precedente et fenetre courante -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> difference bin a bin -> norme euclidienne
It is useful for detecting spectral changes, texture boundaries, transitions and some event onsets. It is often relevant to a future segmentation assistance interface.
Spectral Rolloff finds the frequency below which a specified percentage of cumulative spectral energy lies. The current threshold comes from the settings, often around 85 or 90 percent.
Signal mono -> fenetre d'analyse -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> somme cumulee -> frequence au seuil
It indicates the effective spectral extent. Use it to track spectral expansion, filtering, brightness and transitions between low sounds and sounds rich in high frequencies.
Spectral Standard Deviation measures frequency dispersion around the spectral centroid. It is the square root of spectral variance.
Signal mono -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> centroide spectral -> variance ponderee -> racine carree
It helps distinguish concentrated spectra from broad spectra. It can reveal changes in spectral width independently of overall level.
Spectral Variance measures the squared dispersion of the spectrum around the centroid. A high value indicates energy spread far from the spectral center.
Signal mono -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> centroide spectral -> dispersion quadratique ponderee
Use it to observe overall spectral width. It can help compare narrow sounds, such as whistles or resonances, with broader or noisier sounds.
Zero Crossing Rate counts sign changes in the time-domain frame. The result is normalized by the number of possible transitions.
Signal mono -> fenetre temporelle -> signes successifs -> comptage des passages par zero
It is sensitive to high frequencies, noisy textures and unstable signals. It can help distinguish low, stable sounds from noisy sounds or sounds rich in high frequencies.
Average Deviation measures the mean absolute deviation of samples from their mean. In iAnalyse, it is computed on the time-domain signal.
Signal mono -> fenetre temporelle -> moyenne -> ecart absolu moyen

It provides a simple indication of amplitude variability within a frame. It can complement RMS to distinguish regular frames from more fluctuating ones, but it has not been aligned with the LibXtract/Sonic Visualiser output.

Inharmonicity estimates how far the spectrum deviates from multiples of an approximate fundamental. The fundamental is estimated from the strongest non-DC spectral bin. Each bin then contributes its distance from the nearest harmonic multiple, weighted by squared amplitude.
Signal mono -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> estimation f0 par pic maximal -> ecart aux harmoniques -> moyenne ponderee
Use it to observe a sound’s degree of inharmonicity. It is relevant to distinguishing harmonic sounds, bells, metallic percussion, complex textures and timbral transformations.
Spectral Kurtosis measures the concentration or peakedness of the spectral distribution around the centroid. A high value indicates a distribution with pronounced peaks or tails.
Signal mono -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> centroide -> variance -> moment d'ordre 4 normalise
It helps characterize highly concentrated spectra, resonances or sounds with a few dominant components. It can complement variance and crest to describe spectral shape.
Loudness is a simple perceptual approximation based on RMS. It applies power-law compression to bring the measure closer to perceived level.
Signal mono -> fenetre temporelle -> RMS -> compression par puissance
Use it to follow perceived dynamics rather than strictly linear energy. It can help visualize changes in intensity or dynamic contrasts.
Noisiness is a proxy derived from Harmonic Ratio. The less periodic the signal, the greater its noisiness.
Signal mono -> fenetre temporelle -> harmonic ratio par autocorrelation -> complement a 1
It can help track the noisy or unstable component of a signal. It is useful for distinguishing noisy textures from periodic sounds, but remains an experimental proxy.

Spectral Skewness measures the asymmetry of the spectral distribution around the centroid. A positive value indicates a distribution extending more toward high frequencies; a negative value indicates an extension toward low frequencies.
Signal mono -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> centroide -> ecart-type -> moment d'ordre 3 normalise
It helps reveal which side of the centroid the spectral energy extends toward. It can be useful for observing timbral shifts or asymmetric filtering.

Spectral Sharpness estimates perceptual brightness by giving greater weight to high frequencies. The current version is a direct approximation over FFT bins, rather than a full psychoacoustic Bark-band decomposition.
Signal mono -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> conversion frequence en kHz -> ponderation hautes frequences -> moyenne ponderee
Use it to track brightness, high-frequency attacks, filtering and changes in timbral color. It is especially useful for sounds whose perception strongly depends on high-frequency energy.
Spectral Slope estimates the linear slope of the spectrum on a frequency axis normalized between 0 and 1. The result is adjusted to remain readable in the data display.
Signal mono -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> axe frequentiel normalise -> regression lineaire normalisee
It shows whether the spectrum tilts toward low or high frequencies. It can reveal filtering, changes in spectral density or prominent peaks in brightness.
Spectral Smoothness measures local spectral irregularity by comparing each bin with the logarithmic mean of its neighbors. A low value indicates a locally regular spectrum.
Signal mono -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> log magnitudes -> comparaison locale aux voisins -> moyenne absolue
Use it to track spectral regularity or irregularity. It can help distinguish smooth, noisy, grainy or strongly resonant spectra.
Spectral Contrast divides the spectrum into logarithmic bands and measures the relative difference between the highest and lowest value in each band. The result is the mean of the band contrasts.
Signal mono -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> bandes logarithmiques -> peak/valley par bande -> moyenne
It can describe a spectrum’s clarity or internal contrast. In musical analysis, it can help identify changes in texture, density or separation between components.
Spectral Reflux measures only magnitude increases between two consecutive spectra. Decreases in energy are ignored.
Fenetre precedente et courante -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> difference positive bin a bin -> norme euclidienne
It is useful for identifying emerging spectral components, attacks, component entries or sudden spectral enrichment. It can complement Spectral Flux in a segmentation interface.
Spectral Entropy converts magnitudes into a probability distribution, then computes normalized Shannon entropy. A high value indicates energy spread over many bins.
Signal mono -> FFT magnitudes lineaires -> normalisation en probabilites -> entropie de Shannon normalisee
It helps distinguish concentrated, pitched or resonant spectra from diffuse or noisy spectra. It is relevant to tracking changes in texture or density.
Harmonic Ratio measures signal periodicity through autocorrelation. It finds the highest normalized correlation for lags corresponding approximately to fundamental frequencies between 50 and 2000 Hz.
Signal mono -> fenetre temporelle -> autocorrelation normalisee -> maximum dans la plage de lags
Use it to track periodicity or the tonal character of a sound. It differs from an odd/even harmonics ratio, which compares even and odd harmonics after estimating partials.
Attack Time measures, within each frame, the time between reaching 10% and 90% of the local absolute maximum. This is a frame-based version, not an event-based measure relying on onset detection.
Signal mono -> fenetre temporelle -> enveloppe absolue simple -> seuils 10% et 90% -> duree
It can provide a local indication of attack speed. For more robust analysis, a future version could measure attacks around detected events.
Onset Strength measures the positive increase in RMS between the previous and current frames. It is therefore a simple energy-based onset strength measure.
Fenetre precedente et courante -> RMS temporel -> difference positive
It can help identify attacks or increases in energy. It is simpler than spectral methods, but can still be useful in a segmentation interface.
Stereo Balance measures the energy balance between the first two channels. The output is normalized for display: 0 means left, 0.5 center and 1 right.
Canaux gauche/droit -> fenetres synchronisees -> RMS gauche et RMS droit -> balance signee -> normalisation 0...1
Use it to visualize left-right movement or imbalance. It does not measure stereo width, correlation or phase.
MID/SIDE Ratio measures the proportion of side energy in the stereo signal. A low value indicates a centered or mono signal; a high value indicates a wide or strongly lateral signal.
Canaux gauche/droit -> transformation MID/SIDE -> RMS mid et side -> ratio side / total
Use it to track stereo width, spatialization effects and more or less centered passages. It complements Stereo Balance, which measures left-right position.

This page describes the main audio representations computed by iAnalyse: linear and logarithmic spectrograms, chromagram, MFCC, spectral complexity spectrogram, logarithmic-resolution representation (“wavelet”), stereo spatial spectrograms, fundamental frequency, descriptor graphs, and the self-similarity matrix. The aim is to explain the actual pipeline, how parameters affect the image, and musical uses, rather than to derive every formula. A representation is never a neutral transcription of sound: window, hop, scale and dynamic-range settings emphasize some phenomena while hiding others.

In every time-based image: the horizontal axis represents time; the vertical axis represents frequency, pitch, pitch class or coefficient index, depending on the representation; color or brightness generally represents normalized energy; each image column corresponds to an analysis frame, not a durationless instant. The common pipeline is: Audio file -> signal decoding and conversion -> channel selection or mixing -> division into overlapping frames -> multiplication by an analysis window -> FFT at 44,100 Hz -> optional frequency filtering -> representation-specific transformation -> normalization and image conversion -> display palette, dynamics and transparency Computation and display are separate stages. Changing the palette or display dynamics does not necessarily recompute the analysis; changing window size, hop, spectral type or its parameters produces new data.

For a multichannel source, iAnalyse lets you choose a specific channel or a mix of the channels. Spatial spectrograms always use the first two channels. Setting Effect on the visualization Musical uses and precautions Mix Combines channels into a mono signal Convenient overview, but components in phase opposition may be attenuated Isolated channel Displays only one channel Useful for comparing a recording, track or side of the stereo field Two spatial channels Keeps left and right separate Required to analyze panning, width and decorrelation

Window size determines the fundamental trade-off between temporal and frequency precision. Small window -> temporally sharp attacks -> broader, less precise frequencies Large window -> better-separated frequencies and partials -> attacks spread over time At 44,100 Hz, a window of 2,048 samples lasts about 46 ms, and the FFT bin spacing is about 21.5 Hz. Choice Visual appearance Musical uses favored Small window Sharp transients, broad frequency bands Percussion, articulation, fast rhythms, segmentation Medium window Readable compromise General analysis, timbre, mixed textures Large window Fine harmonic lines, blurred event timing Sustained pitches, beating, neighboring partials, low resonances A very large window does not create information: it improves frequency separation by averaging over a longer duration.

In iAnalyse, the effective hop is proportional to window size: hop = window size × hop setting / 10 The default setting of 7 therefore advances by 70% of the window, giving 30% overlap. Hop Visual appearance Analytical consequence Small Many columns, smoother transitions Better temporal tracking, greater computation and storage needs Large More discontinuous or coarse image Fast computation, but brief events may fall between frames The hop changes the analysis’s temporal sampling, not the intrinsic frequency resolution of each FFT.

The analysis window attenuates the edges of each frame to limit spectral leakage. Window family Expected appearance Suggested use Rectangular Narrow peaks but strong leakage around frequencies not aligned with bins Special measurements on very stable signals Hann/Hanning Good compromise, smooth appearance Recommended general choice Hamming Controlled sidelobes, resolution close to Hann General analysis of tonal signals Blackman and strongly tapered windows Cleaner background around strong peaks, broader peaks Finding weak components near strong ones The exact names of the available windows depend on the application’s menu. Their common role is to set the balance between peak sharpness and spectral leakage.

Dynamic range determines the gap between the strongest components and the lowest level retained in the image. Value Visual effect Musical use Short range, for example −40 dB High contrast; only strong components remain visible Fundamentals, dominant attacks, clear structural reading Medium range, for example −60 to −80 dB Balance between detail and readability Timbre, resonances, general analysis Long range, for example −100 dB Many weak details and more noise Decays, reverberation, hiss, secondary components An extended range can give background noise excessive visual prominence. Do not confuse it with the work’s overall musical dynamics.

Optional filters zero out regions of the spectrum before representation-specific transformations. Note the current internal terminology: activateLowPass removes the lower region up to the chosen frequency, while activateHighPass removes the upper region from the chosen frequency onward. In the interface, check the visual effect rather than relying solely on the field’s technical name. Setting Visual effect Musical use Remove low frequencies Removes DC, hum and low-frequency energy Examine attacks, noise and the high register Remove high frequencies Removes hiss and high components Examine fundamentals, bass and dark masses Filtering affects the analysis: removed content no longer contributes to subsequent calculations, including chromagrams, MFCCs and spatial representations.

The palette maps numerical values to colors. It adds no acoustic information. Display parameter Effect Recommendation Multicolor palette Visually separates several levels Useful for exploring energy in detail, but may suggest false categorical thresholds Two-color or monochrome palette More restrained intensity display Useful for comparing representations or printing Display dynamics Lightens or darkens already computed data Adjust without confusing this with FFT dynamic range in dB Transparent background Makes overlays easier Check contrast against annotations and other layers Keep the same palette and settings when comparing excerpts. Different palettes can make two spectra look more different than they are.

The linear spectrogram stacks successive FFT magnitudes on a vertical axis uniformly graduated in hertz. Signal -> overlapping frames -> analysis window -> FFT and logarithmic dynamic-range conversion -> optional filters -> vertical reduction for the image -> time × linear-frequency spectrogram Equal pixel distances correspond to equal intervals in hertz. A 1,000 Hz band therefore occupies the same height in the low and high registers.
This type has no additional spectral parameter: its behavior mainly depends on window size, hop, window type, dynamic range, channel and filters.

horizontal lines: stable partials or resonances; vertical lines: attacks and impulsive events; broad clouds: noise or wideband texture; curves: glissandi, pitch drift or filter sweeps; halos after events: reverberation or resonance.

The linear spectrogram is especially suited to analyzing timbre, spectral orchestration, filtering and high-frequency content. It shows the physical spacing of partials clearly and supports measurements in hertz. It is less convenient for following musical pitches in the bass: low octaves occupy very little height, while high frequencies take up much of the image.

The logarithmic spectrogram starts from the FFT and redistributes bins along an axis close to musical pitch: each octave occupies a comparable height. Signal -> frames -> FFT -> optional contrast -> frequency-to-logarithmic-pitch projection -> energy threshold -> time × pitch spectrogram This projection makes intervals, registers and harmonic structures easier to read.

Parameter Effect on the image Musical use Contrast: none, medium, high, maximum Progressively emphasizes maxima and attenuates intermediate values Separates harmonic lines; strong contrast may erase noise, reverberation and weak partials A frequency (aFreq, default 440 Hz) Shifts pitch-grid alignment Adapt the analysis to historical tuning, a different overall tuning or an out-of-tune source Threshold (threshold, default 0.4) Removes components below a relative level Cleans the image; an excessive value creates a false impression of a sparse spectrum or silence Minimum frequency/pitch Crops the bottom and expands the remaining register Exclude DC and sub-bass; focus on the instrumental register Maximum frequency/pitch Crops the top and expands the remaining register Focus on useful fundamentals and harmonics, or include high-frequency noise The note and octave fields describe musical bounds; the lower and upper frequencies are their numerical equivalents used in computation.

This view is recommended for following melodies, chords, registers, glissandi and harmonic series over several octaves. Transposed patterns retain a comparable vertical geometry. It is not note detection: each harmonic remains visible and may be mistaken for a fundamental. Precision in the bass still depends on FFT window size.

This representation applies a bank of bands evenly spaced in octaves to FFT magnitudes. Two algorithms are available: triangular Constant-Q filters and Morlet-shaped filters. It is a logarithmic-resolution time-frequency representation built from an FFT, not a full time-domain wavelet transform. Signal -> frames -> FFT in dB -> frequency filters -> logarithmic band bank between fmin and fmax -> thresholding -> gamma correction -> interpolation of missing bands -> vertical smoothing -> time × bands-per-octave image

Parameter Effect on the visualization Musical use and trade-offs Triangular Constant-Q algorithm More localized bands and sharper rendering Reading pitches, partials and attacks; fast and stable Morlet algorithm Softer, overlapping bands Continuous textures, glissandi, masses and transitions; slightly softened attacks Minimum frequency, default 27.5 Hz Sets the image’s lower bound and total band count Including deep bass requires a sufficiently long window; otherwise low bands become sparse or unstable Maximum frequency, default 7,040 Hz Sets the image’s upper bound Lowering it focuses on pitches/partials; raising it includes noise, hiss and brightness Bands per octave, default 40, range 6…48 Sets vertical density High values: fine intervals and detailed glissandi, but a taller image and a risk of bands without FFT support Quality, default 12, range 2…32 For Morlet, narrows filters around their center frequency High: better partial separation but more discontinuous rendering; low: smoother envelopes but merged neighboring frequencies Threshold, default 0.02, range 0…1 Removes and then rescales weak magnitudes Cleans noise and reverberation; too high, it erases weak partials and sound endings Gamma, default 0.4, range 0.25…4 Nonlinear curve after thresholding Above 1: weak values become more visible; below 1: greater contrast and darker background Vertical smoothing, default 1, range 0…4 Repeatedly averages neighboring bands Reduces striping; too strong, it merges nearby pitches and partials

Bands per octave cannot exceed the resolution provided by the FFT. With a short window, greatly increasing this setting adds interpolation or smoothing rather than revealing new information, especially in the bass. For precise low frequencies, increase window size before vertical density. Quality only affects the Morlet profile. Threshold, gamma and smoothing control readability: they strongly affect appearance and must remain identical in comparisons.

This view suits pitches over a wide range, partials, glissandi, micro-intervals, resonances and electroacoustic textures. It provides a more musical reading of register than the linear spectrogram while retaining more spectral information than a chromagram.

The chromagram folds all pitches separated by octaves into twelve pitch classes. All Cs, for example, contribute to the same row. Signal -> frames -> FFT -> contrast -> frequency-to-pitch conversion -> grouping by pitch class modulo the octave -> threshold and optional RMS-energy modulation -> time × 12 pitch-class image

Parameter Effect on the image Musical use Contrast Makes dominant classes more distinct Clarifies chords and tonalities; may hide passing notes and harmonic enrichments A frequency Aligns classes with the actual tuning reference Essential for archives, historical instruments or nonstandard tuning Threshold Removes weak contributions Stabilizes chords; too high, it removes weak thirds, extensions and resonances Low frequency (lowFreq, default 15 Hz) Excludes very low frequencies from folding Prevents DC, impacts and rumble from contaminating classes High frequency (highFreq, default 14,080 Hz) Limits the upper harmonics included Reduces noise and cymbals; too low a limit removes useful harmonic evidence Energy modulation Weights classes by the frame’s relative RMS Preserves dynamics and distinguishes weak/strong regions; when disabled, harmonic reading is less level-dependent Modulation uses the file’s maximum RMS as its reference. An exceptionally loud event may therefore make the rest of the piece appear visually weaker.

The chromagram is useful for analyzing harmony, chord progressions, pitch centers, tonality, ostinatos and repetitions transposed by octaves. It is robust to register changes. It deliberately discards octave, register, partial order and much timbral information. It works less well with noise, untuned percussion, dense multiphonics and inharmonic sounds. A strong class does not prove that a note of that name was played: it may result from several harmonics.

Despite its internal English name, “Complex Spectrogram”, this representation does not display the complex part of the FFT. It represents the difference between two consecutive spectra. Previous frame -> FFT -> magnitudes A Current frame -> FFT -> magnitudes B | -> bin-by-bin difference -> mode selection -> min-max normalization -> time × frequency image

Mode Values retained Appearance and musical use All Increases and decreases Overall view of spectral change; useful for transitions and texture boundaries Increase Emerging or growing energy Attacks, instrumental entries, filter opening, new bands Decrease Disappearing or declining energy Decays, releases, filter closing, resonance endings

A small hop compares nearby moments: differences are finer and more continuous. A large hop emphasizes changes but mixes several events. A small window favors transients; a large window makes slow spectral changes more readable.
documents.s: Impact of hop and window size

documents.t: This representation is very useful for segmentation, studying attacks, texture transitions, articulation and gradual transformations. It answers “where and in which bands does the spectrum change?” rather than “which frequencies are present?”. Per-frame normalization can make a small change as bright as a large one. Compare the geometry and location of changes; do not interpret color as an absolute quantity across columns.

Two synchronized images are computed: mono-mix energy and the left-right position of each spectral bin. Left channel L -> FFT magnitude L --+ -> R / (L + R) by frequency Right channel R -> FFT magnitude R --+ (L + R) / 2 -> FFT in dB -> energy layer energy layer + position layer -> spatial coloring The spatial value is approximately 0 on the left, 0.5 in the center and 1 on the right. At least two channels are required; the first two are used.

Parameter Effect Musical use Left, center and right colors Encode component pan positions Identify lateralized instruments and movement Full mode Combines the entire balance Overview of the spectral mix Left only Visually isolates the left region Examine a lateralized source or event Center only Isolates balanced components Voice, bass, kick drum or centrally placed elements Right only Visually isolates the right region Symmetrical comparison with the left channel Window size and hop have the same effects as in the linear spectrogram. A large window stabilizes sustained-sound positions; a small window better follows rapid movement and attacks.

This view helps analyze spatial orchestration, panning, left-right dialogues, trajectories and the mix’s frequency distribution. It does not by itself measure perceptual width or phase: two decorrelated signals of equal energy may appear centered under this ratio.

The signal is transformed into central and lateral components: MID = (L + R) / 2 SIDE = (L - R) / 2 MID -> FFT magnitude --+ -> SIDE / (MID + SIDE) by frequency SIDE -> FFT magnitude --+ MID -> FFT in dB -> energy layer A low value indicates mainly MID content; a high value indicates mainly SIDE content.

Mode What it highlights Musical use Full MID/SIDE ratio across the spectrum Overview of spectral width MID only Content common to both channels Central sources and mono-compatible elements Balance only Intermediate ratio region Mixtures neither strictly central nor strongly lateral SIDE only Difference between channels Stereo reverberation, width, phase effects, doubling and ambience MID, balance and SIDE colors provide a qualitative legend. They do not replace calibrated correlation or mono-compatibility measurements.

This representation helps study mix width by frequency, visually separate center and ambience, identify spatialization effects or assess what may disappear in a mono downmix. Strong SIDE content may result from spatial placement, reverberation, delay, phase inversion or genuinely different channel content. The image shows the spectral result, not its cause.

MFCCs summarize the perceptual spectral envelope. They describe overall timbral shape more than individual frequencies. Signal -> frames -> FFT -> triangular filter bank on the Mel scale -> energy in each band -> logarithm -> discrete cosine transform (DCT-II) -> 48 coefficients -> replacement of invalid values and per-frame min-max normalization -> time × coefficient-index image The vertical axis is neither frequency nor pitch. Low-order coefficients describe broad envelope shapes; higher-order coefficients describe finer details and are often less stable.

Parameter Effect on the image Musical use Minimum frequency Removes the influence of low bands below the bound Avoid rumble and DC, or isolate an instrument’s useful range Maximum frequency Removes bands above the bound Reduce hiss/cymbals or target an instrumental family Number of Mel bands (numMelBands, default 18) Changes the detail of the spectral summary before the DCT Few bands: stable overall shape; more bands: finer timbral details but greater sensitivity to noise and FFT settings The current implementation produces 48 coefficients. The number of Mel bands controls the input filter bank, not directly the number of final rows.

Window size is crucial: a small window follows articulation changes quickly, while a large window stabilizes timbral color. Since each frame is min-max normalized, the view mainly highlights the internal coefficient shape rather than absolute level differences over time.

MFCCs suit timbre comparison, detection of changes in instrumentation, playing techniques, phonemes and textures, and automatic segmentation. Similar visual patterns indicate similar spectral envelopes. They are less suitable for directly reading notes or partials. An individual coefficient is difficult to interpret musically: the main value lies in the vector’s shape and evolution. Use exactly the same parameters when comparing files.

The fundamental-frequency representation estimates the signal’s dominant periodicity in each frame. It produces a pitch curve over time rather than a complete spectral image. Signal -> overlapping frames -> period estimation using YIN, MPM or autocorrelation -> period-to-frequency conversion -> range, confidence and amplitude checks -> optional octave-error correction -> removal of isolated values and overly short segments -> median filtering -> time × fundamental-frequency curve Fundamental frequency, commonly written F0, is the signal’s main repetition rate. For a periodic monophonic source, it is generally related to perceived pitch even when the first harmonic is weak or missing. It must not be confused with the strongest frequency in the spectrum.

Parameter Effect on the curve Musical use and precautions YIN algorithm Finds a period from differences between the signal and delayed versions of itself Robust general choice for voice and monophonic instruments; the default algorithm MPM algorithm Finds peaks in a normalized difference function Tracks periodic sounds and their variations well; may react differently from YIN to attacks and overtone-rich timbres Autocorrelation Finds the delay at which the signal most closely resembles itself Intuitive and effective for stable sounds; more prone to confusion between fundamentals and harmonics Minimum and maximum frequencies, default 27.5–3,520 Hz Limit the periods searched and values retained Restricting the range to the source’s tessitura reduces errors and computation A frequency, default 440 Hz Controls conversion between frequency and MIDI pitch Adapt it to the recording’s tuning, especially for historical or detuned instruments Confidence threshold, default 0.2 Rejects estimates whose periodicity is insufficiently certain A high value cleans the curve but may interrupt noisy, breathy or weak sounds Amplitude threshold, default −80 dB Rejects frames that are too quiet Avoids phantom pitches in silence and background noise; too high a threshold cuts note endings Octave-error correction Moves an estimate to the octave closest to the previous value Stabilizes continuous melodic lines; may incorrectly alter a genuine octave leap Maximum interval, default 7 semitones Helps reject an isolated value far from its neighbors Reduces one-frame errors; increase it for music with fast, wide leaps Median-filter size, default 3 frames Locally replaces pitches with their median Removes spikes; a large value also smooths vibrato, trills and ornaments Minimum duration, default 0.03 s Removes voiced segments shorter than the selected duration Rejects fleeting detections; may remove genuinely brief notes or attacks

A long window contains several low-frequency periods and improves their estimation, but smooths attacks and rapid changes. A short window follows articulation more closely but may be insufficient for low pitches. Hop controls the temporal density of the curve: a small hop gives more continuous tracking at greater computational cost.
documents.s: Impact of window size and hop

documents.t: This view is useful for melodic tracking, intonation, vibrato, glissandi, tessitura and octave errors. It is most reliable with a clean monophonic source. In a chord, multiphonic, percussion sound or very noisy signal, the algorithm must select a single periodicity and may return an absent pitch, a subharmonic or no value. A gap in the curve therefore means “no estimate retained”, not necessarily silence.

The descriptor graph reduces each signal frame to one or more numerical measurements, then plots their evolution over time. Unlike a spectrogram, each curve answers a specific acoustic question. Signal -> overlapping frames -> FFT and/or time-domain calculation -> one descriptor vector per frame -> one time series per selected descriptor -> a separate scale and color for each series -> time × value graph The illustration combines three complementary descriptors: spectral centroid, RMS amplitude and zero-crossing rate (ZCR).

Descriptor What it measures Musical reading Spectral centroid The spectrum’s center of gravity, in hertz A high value generally corresponds to a brighter sound with more high-frequency energy; a low value to a darker sound RMS amplitude The signal’s root-mean-square energy within the frame Follows the amplitude envelope: attacks, accents, crescendos, decays and level contrasts ZCR — zero-crossing rate The proportion of sign changes in the signal Often increases with noise, dry attacks and high-frequency content; remains low for low, periodic sounds These measurements are complementary but not independent. A noisy attack may raise RMS, ZCR and spectral centroid at the same time. Their joint evolution is therefore more informative than assigning a single cause to each peak.

Channel, window size, hop and window type behave as in the spectral representations. A small window reveals rapid variations but produces more irregular curves; a large window reveals broad trends and attenuates brief events. Each series retains its own unit and range: hertz for centroid, normalized amplitude for RMS, and a ratio from 0 to 1 for ZCR. The visual heights of two curves therefore do not directly compare their numerical values. Colors identify the series; they do not encode an additional measurement.

This representation is useful for segmentation and for studying articulation, dynamics, brightness, and contrasts between periodic and noisy sounds. It also reveals correlations, such as increasing brightness during a crescendo. A descriptor strongly condenses the signal: perceptually different sounds may share the same centroid, RMS or ZCR. RMS is not a calibrated measure of perceived loudness, centroid does not describe the complete spectral envelope, and ZCR depends on frequency as well as noisiness. Compare the curves with a spectrogram and with listening.

The stream graph combines three time series in one continuous shape. One descriptor controls the ribbon’s vertical position, another its width, and a third its color. Descriptor 1 -> normalization -> vertical center position Descriptor 2 -> normalization -> ribbon width Descriptor 3 -> normalization -> interpolation between two colors | -> continuous shape over time In the illustration: spectral centroid controls vertical position; RMS amplitude controls width; ZCR controls the color between the two selected hues. The result simultaneously shows brightness, energy and periodic or noisy character: a brighter passage moves the ribbon, a more energetic passage widens it, and a rise in ZCR changes its color.

Parameter Visual effect Interpretation precaution Position descriptor Moves the center of the ribbon vertically Top and bottom indicate relative descriptor values, not musical pitch unless a pitch descriptor is selected Width descriptor Thickens or thins the ribbon around its center A large width means a high value of the selected descriptor, not necessarily greater loudness Color descriptor Interpolates between the start and end colors Hue encodes a continuous value; it does not define acoustic categories Start and end colors Define the two extremes of the color range Keep the same colors when comparing stream graphs Center-line display Shows or hides the path of the position descriptor Useful for reading the trajectory precisely when the ribbon becomes wide Line width Changes only the center-line stroke A graphical setting with no effect on computed data The three series are mapped to display-appropriate scales. This normalization highlights their internal evolution, but does not turn different physical quantities into directly comparable measurements.

A small hop and short window produce a responsive, detailed and sometimes jagged ribbon. A longer window and larger hop produce a steadier stream suited to texture evolution, but may absorb brief attacks. All three dimensions must use the same temporal settings to remain synchronized.
documents.s: Impact of window size and hop

documents.t: The stream graph provides a compact reading of gestures, textures, density and timbral trajectories. With the illustrated settings, it reveals bright, loud and noisy areas and the transitions between them at a glance. This view favors synthesis over measurement: area, position and color are perceived differently and may give unequal visual weight to the three descriptors. The same shape may also result from different acoustic phenomena. For precise measurement, return to the separate descriptor graph and inspect the numerical values.

The self-similarity matrix compares every analyzed moment with every other moment in the same file. Both axes therefore represent time. Each cell indicates how closely the corresponding frames resemble one another according to the selected data and algorithm. Signal -> overlapping frames -> FFT vector or audio-descriptor vector for each frame -> reduction to 1,024, 2,048 or 4,096 moments -> comparison of every pair of vectors -> global normalization and value inversion -> time × time image The matrix is symmetrical: comparing moment A with moment B gives the same value as comparing B with A. Its main diagonal compares each frame with itself and is a visual reference, not a particular musical event.

Parameter Effect on the image Musical use and precautions FFT source Compares the complete spectra of the frames Sensitive to pitches, partials and spectral distribution; useful for repeated patterns whose timbre and register remain close Audio-descriptor source Compares the features selected in the descriptor settings Targets resemblance in level, brightness, dominant frequency or timbre; the result depends entirely on the enabled descriptors Dot product Measures the vectors’ alignment and common amplitude Favors passages with comparable content and level; sensitive to overall energy Euclidean distance Measures overall difference, strongly weighting large discrepancies Good general choice for distinguishing spectral or timbral states Manhattan distance Adds absolute component-by-component differences More progressive when many small differences are distributed across the vector Minkowski distance Uses a power of 4 here, emphasizing the largest differences Highlights changes concentrated in a few dominant components Cosine similarity Mainly compares vector orientation Better recognizes a similar spectral shape despite an overall level difference Definition: 1×, 2× or 4× Produces a matrix 1,024, 2,048 or 4,096 pixels square Higher definition localizes brief structures more precisely but greatly increases computation time and data size With the audio-descriptor source, the normalization selected in the associated settings is applied separately to each descriptor series before comparison. This is especially important when a vector combines quantities with very different units.

main diagonal: each moment’s identity with itself; diagonals parallel to the main diagonal: a sequence repeated after a delay; square blocks: complete homogeneous or recurring sections; horizontal and vertical lines: a passage resembling many other moments, such as a sustained sound, ostinato or stable texture; boundaries and contrasting regions: changes in material, timbre, register or dynamics, depending on the selected source. The distance between a secondary diagonal and the main diagonal represents the delay between two occurrences. Its length indicates how long their evolution remains comparable.

Window size and hop determine what a “moment” means in the matrix. A small window and hop follow brief events more closely but make the matrix more sensitive to attacks and local fluctuations. A large window stabilizes comparisons of sustained textures and harmonies at the cost of less precise temporal boundaries. Channel and frequency filters modify vectors before comparison. Two passages may therefore appear similar within a filtered register without being similar across the full spectrum. To compare matrices visually, retain the same source, algorithm, definition, and FFT or descriptor settings.

The self-similarity matrix is suited to studying form, returns, refrains, ostinatos, sequences, recurring textures and section changes. It provides an overview of temporal relationships that time-frequency representations show less directly. It does not explain the cause of a resemblance and does not automatically recognize a transposed, reorchestrated or strongly varied repetition. Since values are normalized across the whole matrix, color expresses a relationship relative to the analyzed file, not an absolute similarity score comparable between files. Finally, the number of comparisons grows with the square of the definition: moving from 1× to 2× multiplies the work by approximately four, and moving from 1× to 4× by sixteen.

Analytical question Suggested representation Starting settings Where are attacks and noise masses? Linear spectrogram Short to medium window, medium dynamic range Which partials and resonances make up the timbre? Linear or logarithmic resolution Medium to long window, low threshold How do register, melody or glissandi evolve? Logarithmic or logarithmic resolution Bounds suited to the range, medium window Which chords or pitch centers dominate? Chromagram Correct tuning reference; modulation according to the desired prominence of dynamics Where does timbre or instrumentation change? MFCC or complexity Short hop, identical parameters throughout the piece Where do spectral bands appear or disappear? Complexity Increase or decrease mode, short hop How do melody, intonation or vibrato evolve? Fundamental frequency Restricted range, bass-appropriate window, moderate thresholds How do energy, brightness and noisiness evolve separately? Audio descriptor graph RMS, spectral centroid and ZCR; short to medium window How can several evolutions be combined in a compact view? Stream graph Map three complementary descriptors to position, width and color How is the spectrum distributed left-right? Stereo balance Two channels, full mode followed by isolated regions What belongs to the center or to the width? MID/SIDE Full mode, then MID and SIDE separately Where are repetitions and large-scale sections? Self-similarity matrix Source and measure suited to the phenomenon; start at 1× definition

Define the musical question before choosing a representation. Set window size and hop first: they determine the available information. Choose frequency bounds according to register and material. Then adjust contrast, threshold, gamma or smoothing to make that information readable. Keep all parameters unchanged when comparing passages or files. Check a hypothesis in at least two complementary views and by listening. A good setting makes the phenomenon under study stable under small adjustments. If a structure disappears after a slight threshold or palette change, interpret it cautiously.

A bright line is not necessarily a fundamental: it may be a harmonic or resonance. A dark region does not always mean silence: it may result from threshold, dynamic range or frequency bounds. A more detailed image is not necessarily more accurate; it may be noisier or interpolated. The chromagram deliberately merges octaves. MFCCs have no directly readable frequency axis. Complexity measures a relative difference between frames, not musical complexity in an aesthetic sense. Fundamental frequency is a monophonic estimate: a gap in the curve does not necessarily mean silence. Descriptor curves with similar visual heights may use different units and scales. In the stream graph, position, width and color encode three independent values and must not be confused. Spatial representations describe spectral energy ratios, not absolute acoustic localization. Every analysis depends on the internal sample rate of 44,100 Hz and the Nyquist limit of 22,050 Hz.

This guide connects representations, audio descriptors, score and video annotation, and analytical uses of iAnalyse. It is neither a treatise on musical acoustics nor a fixed analytical method. Its aim is to show how signal processing and multimodal annotation can support musicological work grounded in listening, observation, comparison and interpretation. Technical details of each calculation are presented in: Audio descriptors. Spectral representations. This guide instead starts from the analyst’s questions.

iAnalyse can be understood as an environment for augmented listening. Visualizations and measurements are not intended to generate a work’s musical meaning automatically. They transform the sound signal into observable objects to support six fundamental operations: Navigate files, particularly long recordings. Remember music with overview representations. Identify clues to investigate through listening and musical analysis. Extend the analysis: compare, experiment, make observations explicit, communicate, document and connect with musical practice. Annotate multimedia files, scores, videos and other materials. Build multimedia journeys through musical analysis.

A rigorous approach avoids moving directly from a numerical result to a musicological conclusion. Four levels should be distinguished. Level Question Example Computed data What did the algorithm measure? The spectral centroid increases Observable clue Which acoustic phenomenon could explain this change? Energy shifts toward higher frequencies Musical hypothesis What function might this phenomenon serve? Brightening timbre, increasing density or changing orchestration Interpretation How does this phenomenon act within the work? Preparing a formal articulation or gradually transforming material An increase in centroid does not by itself mean “tension”, “climax” or “expressive brightness”. These concepts result from a contextual interpretation, confirmed through listening and connected to other parameters. The recommended path is: mesure -> observation -> hypothèse -> écoute ciblée -> annotation -> comparaison -> interprétation
documents.s: From signal to interpretation: four distinct levels

documents.t: A spectrogram, chromagram or self-similarity matrix (SSM) preserves several dimensions at once. These views suit exploration, pattern recognition and memorization. They address questions such as: where are significant events? which regions resemble one another? how does register or texture evolve? which structures recur? are there continuous processes, breaks or symmetries?

A descriptor reduces each frame to one or a few values. It lets you follow a chosen dimension precisely, compare passages and look for thresholds or trends. It addresses questions such as: does energy actually increase? does the spectral distribution become higher or broader? does the texture become noisier? does the spectrum change rapidly? does the content become more lateral?

Représentation synoptique -> fait apparaître une forme ou une rupture Descripteur -> précise la dimension acoustique concernée Écoute -> identifie le phénomène musical Annotation -> inscrit l'interprétation dans la temporalité de l'œuvre For example, a break visible in a spectrogram can be checked against spectral flux, RMS and centroid. Listening then helps determine whether it is a new source, a change in playing technique, filtering, an edit or a broader formal articulation.
documents.s: Combining them is more productive than using either alone

documents.t: In a long recording, linear listening alone makes precise returns, comparisons between distant regions and rapid overviews difficult. Representations turn the file into a map of time.

Navigation need Representation or descriptor Clue to look for Identify silence and large masses Waveform, RMS, Loudness Alternating activity/rest, overall level changes Locate attacks Waveform, Onset Strength, Attack Time Impulsive events and sequence beginnings Identify texture changes Spectrogram, complexity, Spectral Flux Breaks or transformations in frequency content Follow register changes Logarithmic spectrogram, Peak Frequency, Spectral Centroid Overall movement toward low or high frequencies Find harmonic regions Chromagram Pitch-class configurations Identify returns SSM, chromagram, MFCC Diagonal patterns or similar blocks Explore spatial evolution Stereo balance, MID/SIDE Movement or width changes

Start with a general view: waveform and spectrogram. Observe large-scale contrasts without immediately trying to name them. Place markers at breaks, thresholds, returns and distinctive regions. Add one or two descriptors corresponding to the main hypothesis. Listen around the markers, including a few seconds before and after. Turn relevant markers into segments or annotations. Return to an overview to check that the segmentation is coherent.

An event’s visibility depends on the settings. An attack may be clear with a short window and disappear with a long one; a low resonance may behave oppositely. Effective navigation may therefore require several maps of the same file.

Listening unfolds over time: what has just been heard must be retained to compare it with what follows. An overview representation makes distant events visible simultaneously. It acts as an external memory of the work. This is particularly important for: long works; music without a score; experimental works; improvisation; soundscapes and field-recording collections; gradual processes that are difficult to segment; comparisons between versions.

A self-similarity matrix, or SSM, compares each moment or segment of the file with every other one. Audio -> extraction de vecteurs par fenêtres -> comparaison de chaque vecteur avec tous les autres -> matrice temps × temps The horizontal and vertical axes represent the same file. The main diagonal corresponds to each moment’s identity with itself. Shape observed in an SSM Hypothesis to check Diagonal line parallel to the main diagonal Repetition or return of a sequence Homogeneous square along the diagonal Relatively stable section Checkerboard or repeated blocks Periodic organization, alternation or recurring form Sharp break between blocks Possible section boundary Interrupted or distorted diagonal Varied, accelerated, slowed or transformed repetition An SSM does not tell you what repeats. Similarity may arise from timbre, energy, harmony or texture, depending on the data used in the comparison.

documents.t: Memorization becomes analytical when connected to annotations: forme visuelle -> écoute du passage -> qualification -> annotation -> relation avec d'autres passages A color or pattern should not substitute for sound. It serves as a reference for recalling a quality heard, function or hypothesis.
documents.s: Build an analytical image, rather than merely recognize an image

documents.t: A clue is an observable fact that may guide analysis without yet constituting proof or a sufficient interpretation. Examples: simultaneous increases in RMS and centroid; a secondary diagonal in an SSM; a stable horizontal band in a spectrogram; a sudden MFCC change; increased SIDE content; a persistent pitch class in a chromagram. A clue becomes musically relevant when it is: precisely located; described without overinterpretation; checked by listening; compared with its context; connected to other clues; integrated into a hypothesis about the work.

A useful practice combines three sources of knowledge: VISUALISATION : où et sous quelle forme le phénomène apparaît-il ? MESURE : quelle dimension varie et dans quelle direction ? ÉCOUTE : qu'entend-on, dans quel contexte et avec quelle fonction ? When they converge, the hypothesis becomes stronger. When they diverge, the divergence is itself informative: it may reveal unsuitable settings, a perceptual limitation or a separation between acoustic dimensions.
The three main functions—navigation, memory and identifying clues—extend into several important uses in digital musicology.

Aligning representations and using common measurements facilitates comparisons between: distant moments in a work; different occurrences of material; performances; versions, edits or restorations; works in the same corpus; different musical or sonic practices. The computer helps make comparison criteria explicit. A resemblance may concern energy, timbre, register, harmony, morphology or space without being an overall similarity. Ressemblance perçue -> choix d'une dimension à comparer -> représentation ou descripteur commun -> contrôle des paramètres et des sources -> écoute comparative -> qualification des invariants et des différences This moves beyond “these passages resemble each other” to ask precisely how, at what scale, and despite which differences.

Visualizations can serve a heuristic function: they sometimes reveal a phenomenon that was not being sought. Examples: spectral regularity unnoticed during initial listening; a transformed return suggested by an SSM diagonal; spatial organization connected to form; a separation between dynamics and brightness; timbral continuity across supposedly distinct sections. Exploration is productive when graphical discovery is distinguished from musical relevance. An unexpected shape becomes a research lead, not a conclusion. A heuristic approach may alternate between: question initiale -> exploration visuelle -> anomalie ou motif inattendu -> nouvelle question -> écoute ciblée -> choix d'une mesure plus spécifique -> reformulation de l'hypothèse

Making observations explicit does not mean eliminating subjectivity. It means stating the operations that lead to an observation: audio source used; passage boundaries; channel or channel mix; window and hop settings; chosen representation and descriptors; thresholds, bounds and normalizations; segmentation or comparison criteria. This information allows another person to reproduce the calculation, discuss the choices and obtain a comparable visualization. It distinguishes computed results, perceptual description and interpretation. Reproducibility strengthens an argument without making the interpretation unique. Two analysts may share observations and propose different musical readings.
documents.s: Function 6 — Make observations explicit and reproducible

documents.t: Overview images, curves and annotations can mediate between the work and different audiences: guide classroom listening; explain an acoustic phenomenon; present the form of a work without a score; connect perceptual vocabulary with signal data; communicate an analytical journey; document a performance or practice-based research. A teaching visualization should be more selective than an exploratory interface. It benefits from few parameters, a clear legend and synchronization with audible examples. The recommended teaching sequence is: écouter sans image -> verbaliser les perceptions -> observer une représentation ciblée -> relier forme visible et phénomène acoustique -> réécouter -> discuter ce que l'image explique et ce qu'elle ne montre pas This alternation avoids letting the image supply the answer in advance or impose a single way of hearing.

iAnalyse preserves stages of reasoning within one temporal workspace: navigation markers; proposed segmentation; descriptive and interpretive annotations; relationships between events; representations that prompted the hypothesis; curves used as evidence; reservations and competing hypotheses. This turns analysis into an inspectable, revisable record. It supports scholarly writing, presentation preparation, collaborative work and analytical editions. A strong argument does more than insert a spectrogram screenshot. It explains what to observe, why the settings are appropriate, how the phenomenon is perceived and how it supports the interpretation.

The same tools can support composition, performance and sound production: compare takes; observe the spectral balance of instrumental playing; study a gesture’s evolution; prepare a performance from articulation points; analyze spatialization or a mix; retrieve and transform material during creative work. Here, computed results can provide feedback: they not only describe a finished work but inform artistic decisions. Measurement remains one perspective among others and does not define an aesthetic standard.
documents.s: Function 9 — Connect analysis and musical practice

documents.t: iAnalyse goes beyond examining the audio signal. Slideshow and Video Documents let you place annotations directly on a score, image or film shot while connecting them with the media’s temporal progression. This changes the status of annotation: annotation temporelle = à quel moment le phénomène se produit-il ? annotation spatiale = où se trouve-t-il dans la partition ou dans l'image ? annotation audiovisuelle = comment sa position, sa durée et son contenu visuel se rapportent-ils à ce qui est entendu ? Multimodal analysis can connect several spaces: recording time; the score’s graphical space; the video frame; editing time; computed sound representations; the conceptual space built by analytical categories and relationships.

A Slideshow Document connects a sequence of slides with media time. Each slide may contain a score image and its own annotations. Playback position determines the displayed page and the objects’ temporal visibility. Audio ou vidéo -> positions temporelles des changements de page -> diapositives contenant les images de partition -> annotations spatiales sur chaque page -> durée d'apparition des annotations -> lecture synchronisée partition / média / commentaire analytique Image zoom and alignment adapt the score to the presentation frame. Annotations remain organized by slide and also appear in the Document’s timeline.

Operation Analytical example Locate Frame a cell, note, chord, motif or indication Connect Show correspondences between voices, motifs, registers or pages Establish hierarchy Distinguish main structure, detail and secondary commentary Place in time Reveal an annotation when the passage is heard Compare Use consistent colors or categories across occurrences Comment Associate text, a symbol or an explanation with a precise region Guide Build a reading path that follows the performance Graphical shapes, lines, text and composite annotations can distinguish levels of discourse: description, segmentation, motivic relationships, harmonic function, orchestration or interpretive hypotheses.

A score annotation has two complementary anchors: a graphical position on the page; a time interval in the recording. This dual placement distinguishes: the written object, which may occupy a stable region of the score; its sonic realization, which has a duration and a place within the performance; the analytical commentary, which may appear before, during or after the event. For a repeat, cadenza, rubato or tempo change, the relationship between notated space and recorded time is nonlinear. Slide changes and annotation durations can document this difference.

Motivic and thematic analysis​ outline occurrences of a motif; use a consistent color for its identity; add a second graphical property for its transformation; connect antecedents and consequents; compare augmentation, diminution, inversion, fragmentation or transposition. Color then represents an analytical category, not a computed acoustic property. Its legend should be explicit. Harmonic and contrapuntal analysis​ annotate chords, functions, voice leading or prolongations; show common tones and chromatic movement; distinguish local and global harmonic levels; follow a pedal point or structural line across pages; reveal analyses during listening. Orchestration analysis​ color instrumental families or orchestral functions; identify doubling, handovers, timbral fusion and contrast; connect notation with the spectrogram and descriptors; compare notated density, sonic density and recorded balance. Performance analysis​ align the score with a specific recording; annotate breathing, rubato, accentuation, phrasing and articulation; compare notated and performed duration; identify choices of balance, dynamics or timbre; prepare comparisons between performances. A crescendo marking in the score, an increase in RMS and perceived intensification are three different objects. Comparing them is precisely what makes it possible to study their realization in performance. Contemporary music and unconventional notation​ comment on symbols, playing techniques and setups; explain open or mobile sections; follow the relationship between prescriptive notation and sonic result; annotate graphic scores; document performers’ decisions.

The Slideshow can become an augmented listening score: page de partition + surlignage synchronisé + commentaire progressif + écoute + possibilité de revenir au contexte Uses include: analysis classes with progressively revealed levels; presenting a motif as it enters; synchronized orchestration commentary; introductions to score reading; lectures or concerts with commentary; performer preparation; introducing a contemporary work; publishing an accessible analytical journey. Effective outreach avoids showing every annotation at once. It organizes a progression: identification, listening, explanation, comparison and synthesis.

The page may suggest that the score is the entire work, relegating performance to the background. Highlighting directs attention toward the analyst’s prior choices. A page change is not necessarily a musical articulation. Synchronization with one recording does not apply to every performance. An annotation placed on a note may concern a phenomenon extending beyond its notation. It is therefore useful to distinguish visually between information from the score, listening, computation and interpretation.

A Video Document overlays graphical annotations whose visibility depends on time. They can identify a region of the frame, comment on an event, follow an object compatible with video tracking, and connect with computed representations. Vidéo avec son -> image courante -> annotations spatiales superposées -> intervalles temporels de visibilité -> suivi éventuel d'un objet dans le cadre -> représentations et données synchronisées -> lecture analytique audiovisuelle The timeline retains annotation intervals. The analyst can therefore work simultaneously with the current image and the overall temporal organization.

Operation Example Identify within the frame Instrument, performer, gesture, object, region or visual detail Delimit in time Shot, movement, entry, action or synchronization Track Keep an annotation on a moving object when tracking applies Connect Associate gesture, sound event and musical change Overlay Compare video, annotation and computed representation Categorize Identify shot types, gestures, sources or functions Export or present Produce a commented audiovisual reading

Analyzing music for moving images involves more than listing synchronizations. It examines relationships between two temporal and expressive organizations. Synchronization​ coincidence between a sound attack and a cut; musical accent on a movement; harmonic change at a shot transition; appearance or disappearance of a sound with a visible source; exact, anticipated, delayed or gradually established synchronization. A synchronization point becomes analytically interesting when its preparation, recurrence and function are also examined. Editing and form​ Visual dimension Musical dimensions to compare Shot duration Phrases, pulse, event density Cut Attack, silence, cadence, spectral break Fade Transition, timbral continuity, resonance Alternating shots Ostinato, periodicity, dialogue, antiphony Long take Continuous process, sustained sound, accumulation Change of shot scale Register, density, dynamics, orchestration The aim is not to reduce the relationship to one-to-one correspondences, but to observe agreement, displacement, tension and independence between editing and music. Point of view, space and listening​ relationship between a source’s position in the frame and its stereo position; off-screen or acousmatic sounds, or sounds with ambiguous sources; changes in listening perspective; sonic continuity across visual discontinuity; diegetic space, off-screen space or musical commentary; depth suggested by reverberation, level or filtering. The stereo balance spectrogram and MID/SIDE ratio can complement frame annotation, but do not alone determine a sound’s narrative or spatial status. Dramaturgical and narrative functions​ continuity or rupture between sequences; anticipation of a visual event; recall or memory association; characterization of a place, character or state; change of narrative level; irony, contradiction or distance between music and image. These functions cannot be computed directly. Measurements help describe the material that realizes them, while audiovisual annotation supports arguments about their contextual role.

Video annotation also opens up the study of music as bodily activity. Instrumental gesture​ preparation, attack, sustain and release; coordination between hands; sound-producing and expressive gestures; relationship between movement amplitude and acoustic result; bodily anticipation of a sound event; playing techniques and technical changes. Interaction​ looks and signals between musicians; conductor–ensemble coordination; imitation and response; turn-taking in improvisation; temporary leadership; relationships between collective movement and musical density. Stage and setup​ performers’ movement; use of interfaces and electronics; relationship with the audience; visible spatial arrangement and heard spatialization; staging, lighting and sound production. Object tracking can keep a graphical reference on a moving element. It does not replace gesture analysis: a geometric trajectory alone does not define musical function.

A video can connect: bodily weight shifts and accents; choreographic and musical phrases; synchronization, counterpoint or independence; movement density and sonic density; spatial occupation and spatialization; repeated gestures and musical recurrences. Annotations can follow bodily regions or events, while markers and segments organize the temporal units being compared.

Beyond film and concert, video annotation is relevant to: audiovisual ethnomusicology; rehearsal observation; analysis of lessons and oral transmission; instrument making and technical gestures; sound installations; interactive setups; studio creation; practice-based research documentation. In these contexts, account for recording conditions, camera angle, what remains off-screen, and the effect of the recording equipment’s presence.

Temporal coincidence does not prove causation. What is visible is not necessarily the source of what is heard. Editing may reconstruct the performance. Framing excludes part of the situation. Automatic tracking may lose the object or drift. An annotation fixed to the frame and one attached to an object do not have the same meaning. Gesture or narrative-function categories must be defined before quantitative comparison.
Slideshow and Video Documents can move beyond individual note-taking to become forms of publication or presentation.

A journey may organize: an initial listening without commentary; an overview of form; several stages focused on specific phenomena; comparative returns; a final integrative listening. Time-based annotations control what appears at each stage. The journey can respect the time needed for discovery rather than immediately presenting a finished analysis.

An edition may combine: facsimile or score; recording; graphical annotations; textual comments; segmentation; acoustic representations; links between occurrences; performance variants. It preserves the distinction between source, observation and commentary while enabling coordinated consultation.

One Document may offer several layers: basic orientation for a first approach; vocabulary and definitions; detailed analysis; questions to solve by listening; delayed display of answers; comparisons between students’ proposals.

In a presentation, synchronized annotations show exactly the passage under discussion. For public outreach, they can make a structure perceptible without requiring prior score reading. In both cases, the visualization should remain readable and its origin explicit: computed data, transcription, analyst’s annotation or source information.

Which gesture prepares or produces the sound event? Which visual clues coordinate performers? How do body, instrument and space contribute to form? What does video show that audio alone cannot establish?

annotations or tracking on relevant bodily and instrumental regions; time intervals for gesture phases; waveform and Onset Strength for attacks; spectrogram for sonic results; segments for interaction units; explicit categories to make observations comparable. Do not confuse visible gesture with acoustic cause. A gesture may prepare, accompany, symbolize or follow a sound without directly producing it.
Where are the articulations? Are there stable sections, transitions or continuous processes? Are boundaries prepared, abrupt or ambiguous? Which parameters change together at each articulation?

Formal function depends on temporal scale and what happens after the peak.

Is the material tonal, noisy, harmonic or inharmonic? How do brightness, density and spectral width evolve? Can families of sounds or playing techniques be distinguished? Is transformation continuous or based on substitutions?
