First describe visible morphology: lines, clouds, bands, impacts, halos. Identify dimensions that seem to vary. Add only descriptors corresponding to those dimensions. Listen to several presumed occurrences of the same family. Annotate similarities and internal differences. Check whether the categories remain relevant in other contexts. MFCCs are useful for finding related timbres, but less explicit for naming them. The spectrogram and listening remain necessary to understand what produces the similarity.

Which pitches or register regions structure the passage? Are there pedal points, pitch centers, aggregates or glissandi? How do chords and pitch classes succeed one another? Do harmonic timbre and perceived pitch converge?

Need Tools Read partials and possible fundamentals Logarithmic spectrogram or logarithmic resolution Follow a dominant frequency Peak Frequency Follow an overall register shift Spectral Centroid and Rolloff Observe pitch classes Chromagram Assess the spectrum’s harmonic organization Harmonic Ratio, Inharmonicity

The spectral peak is not necessarily the fundamental. Centroid describes an energy center, not a musical pitch. The chromagram merges octaves and aggregates harmonics. An inharmonic sound may produce visually strong pitch classes. The reference tuning must match the recording. The best approach often combines logarithmic spectrogram and chromagram: the former preserves register and partials, while the latter summarizes pitch classes.
Where are accumulations, thinning, crescendos and decays? Do level changes coincide with timbral changes? Does a perceived climax arise from amplitude, register, density or their combination?

Phenomenon Tools Average level RMS Amplitude, Loudness Attacks Onset Strength, Attack Time Spectral density Spectrogram, Entropy, Flatness High-frequency extension Centroid, Rolloff, Sharpness Spectral broadening Variance, Standard Deviation

Impression de crescendo -> RMS augmente-t-il ? -> le spectre s'élargit-il ? -> le centroïde monte-t-il ? -> les attaques deviennent-elles plus nombreuses ? -> l'écoute confirme-t-elle une intensification ou seulement un éclaircissement ? Several acoustic trajectories can produce perceived intensification. Describing them separately avoids reducing musical dynamics to sound level alone.
Where do events concentrate? Do attacks form a pulse, gesture or texture? Does activity become more regular, dense or discontinuous?

waveform for visible impacts; Onset Strength for the prominence of event beginnings; Attack Time for their morphology; Spectral Flux for changes between frames; complexity in increase mode to locate emerging bands; Zero Crossing Rate for some noisy or highly active textures. An onset detector does not automatically provide musical rhythm. Peaks must be grouped, hierarchized and interpreted according to tempo, any meter, accentuation and texture.

How are events distributed between left, center and right? Does width vary with register? Which materials belong to the center and which to the lateral environment? Does spatialization contribute to form?

Dimension Representation Descriptor Left/right position by frequency Stereo balance spectrogram Stereo Balance Center versus width MID/SIDE spectrogram MID/SIDE Ratio Overall evolution Curves of both descriptors Comparison with formal segments Representations show where the phenomenon lies spectrally; descriptors summarize its overall trend. Listening on headphones and loudspeakers remains essential. High SIDE content is not necessarily a “sound far to the side”. It may result from reverberation, delay, phase opposition or different channel content.
Does material return unchanged or transformed? What remains invariant: timbre, rhythm, harmony, contour or energy? Can events be grouped into families?

Type of resemblance Preferred tools Timbral MFCC, spectrogram, SSM Harmonic Chromagram, pitch-based SSM Energy-related RMS, Loudness Overall spectral Centroid, Flatness, Rolloff, Entropy Morphological Annotations, visual spectrogram comparison

Use the SSM or an overview to detect a potential resemblance. Isolate the passages and listen to them consecutively. Describe what seems invariant and what varies. Choose descriptors corresponding to those dimensions. Annotate the relationship: repetition, variation, derivation, contrast or simple acoustic resemblance. Acoustic similarity does not imply a common origin or function. Two events can resemble one another without belonging to the same musical material.

To make curves and images comparable, retain: the same sample rate; the same window sizes and types; the same hop; the same frequency bounds; the same thresholds and contrasts; the same palettes and display dynamics; the same channel selection.

recording technique and microphone placement; venue acoustics; mixing and mastering; background noise; dynamic compression; tuning and reference pitch; recording speed or editing. Document these factors. A centroid difference between two performances may arise from playing, but also from microphones or equalization.

documents.t: A work often needs to be observed at several scales. Scale Objects Tools Micro Attack, grain, partial, brief transition Short window, waveform, spectrogram, Onset Meso Gesture, motif, phrase, texture, sequence Spectrogram, chromagram, MFCC, descriptors Macro Section, process, return, overall form SSM, overview images, segments and annotations A strong micro-scale boundary is not necessarily important at the formal scale. identify the source, version and recording conditions; note duration, channels, any reference tuning and file-specific features; formulate an initial musical question.
display waveform and spectrogram; browse the file quickly; place provisional markers; produce an SSM if duration or form justifies it.
listen to identified regions in context; describe what is heard before assigning a function; adjust markers and create segments.
choose a small number of descriptors directly related to the question; keep parameters consistent; identify convergence, divergence and outliers.
turn observations into hypotheses; associate each hypothesis with supporting and contrary evidence; compare occurrences and exceptions.

return to listening without looking at the curves; check that the interpretation remains audible and relevant; actively seek passages that contradict it; reformulate the hypothesis if necessary.

Annotation is where computed data becomes a musicological object. It may contain: the phenomenon’s location; a perceptual description; visual and numerical clues; the analytical hypothesis; degree of certainty; relationships with other events; settings used; objections or alternative interpretations. A useful formulation explicitly separates levels: Observation: simultaneous increases in RMS, centroid and spectral flux between 12:40 and 12:52. Listening: accumulation of layers, gradual opening of the high register and accelerating attacks. Hypothesis: an intensification process preparing the articulation at 12:53. Reservation: the centroid increase may be amplified by the entry of a single high source.
Window, hop, threshold, normalization, bounds and palette construct the observed object. A visualization is a technical interpretation of the signal before it is interpreted musically.

Available descriptors emphasize certain dimensions: energy, spectral distribution, change, harmony or spatiality. They represent phrasing, intention, function, syntax, perceived causality, gesture and cultural meaning less directly.
documents.s: What is measurable does not encompass everything audible

documents.t: A salient graphical shape attracts attention and may lead to overestimating a perceptually minor phenomenon. Alternating listening with and without the display is useful.

A reproducible calculation may rely on a model unsuited to the material. Numerical stability guarantees that the same procedure produces the same result, not that this result is the best musical description.
Two parameters may evolve together without sharing a cause or function. Their relationship must be examined in the work’s context.

Prefer: “the centroid increases” to “the sound becomes tense”; “a similarity appears in the SSM” to “the theme returns”; “pitch class D is dominant” to “the chord is D major”; “the SIDE ratio increases” to “the source moves sideways”; “flux indicates a spectral change” to “a new section begins”. Interpretive wording may follow, supported by arguments that justify moving from one level to another.
How does a long electroacoustic work build its major articulations through timbral transformations?

1. Forme d'onde + spectrogramme -> repérage des grandes masses et silences 2. SSM -> recherche de zones stables, retours et transitions 3. Marqueurs provisoires -> localisation des frontières candidates 4. Flux spectral + RMS + centroïde + flatness -> distinction entre changement d'énergie, de registre et de texture 5. MFCC et spectrogramme de complexité -> observation des transformations timbrales internes 6. Écoute ciblée -> qualification des gestes, matières, continuités et ruptures 7. Segmentation et annotations -> formulation d'une hypothèse formelle 8. Retour à l'écoute intégrale -> vérification de la pertinence perceptive de la segmentation
The result is not a segmentation “discovered” by the algorithm, but an analytical proposal supported by computed, visual and auditory evidence.

From a digital musicology perspective, iAnalyse does more than produce images or curves. It organizes an inquiry into sound: naviguer pour trouver mémoriser pour comparer mesurer pour préciser écouter pour comprendre annoter pour argumenter Representations provide access to overall forms, descriptors isolate acoustic dimensions, and annotations build the bridge to musical analysis. Slideshow Documents place this reasoning on the score; Video Documents extend it to framing, editing, gesture and performance. Their combination supports a practice in which the computer does not conclude on the analyst’s behalf, but helps them see, hear, retrieve, compare, communicate and formulate.
